architect-professional-practice-1.task: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
architect-professional-practice-1.question: A bank's internal CRM agent can read records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. An access review shows account managers only read records and draft emails through it, and auditors flagged the update and delete capabilities as excessive. What is the right change under least privilege?

options.A: Write every update and deletion call to an immutable audit log that the sales operations lead reviews weekly
options.B: Require the account manager to confirm in a dialog before any update or delete tool call is executed
options.C: Restrict the update and delete tools to business hours by scheduling a permission window on the agent
options.D: Remove the update and delete tools from this agent's configuration so its role holds only what it uses

architect-professional-practice-1.rationale: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, which eliminates the error and abuse surface instead of watching it. A weekly log review (A) and a confirmation dialog (B) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and a time window (C) narrows when the risk applies without closing it.
architect-professional-practice-1.evidence: Grant agents only the tools and permissions the task requires; extra capabilities widen the blast radius of mistakes and injections.

architect-professional-practice-2.task: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
architect-professional-practice-2.question: A support team's RAG assistant began giving confident but wrong answers the morning after a nightly document refresh. The pinned model version, the prompts, and the latency dashboards are unchanged, and the refresh job reported success. Where should the architect investigate first?

options.A: How the refresh changed the index: chunk boundaries, embedding consistency, and any mix of stale and new vectors
options.B: Whether the pinned model drifted overnight, by replaying last week's evaluation set against the same model snapshot
options.C: Whether the grounding instructions in the system prompt need tighter wording about citing the retrieved passages
options.D: Whether the retrieved passages are now being truncated by the context budget before they reach the model

architect-professional-practice-2.rationale: The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong answers are the signature of plausible but irrelevant retrieved context, so the index is the first suspect. A pinned model (B) and an unchanged prompt (C) do not correlate with the refresh, and truncation (D) would usually show up as incomplete answers and changed token counts rather than wrong ones.
architect-professional-practice-2.evidence: Retrieval quality depends on how documents are chunked, embedded and indexed; a change there degrades answers even when the model is unchanged.

architect-professional-practice-3.task: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
architect-professional-practice-3.question: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities as tools to agents built by many teams. Loading all forty definitions into every agent's context bloats prompts and degrades tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?

options.A: Rewrite all forty tool descriptions to be shorter, keeping parameters but dropping usage guidance and examples
options.B: Give each agent a small task-relevant toolset and let it find others on demand through tool search or namespaces
options.C: Collapse the forty capabilities into one gateway tool that takes a mode parameter and a free-form payload
options.D: Split the tools between two always-loaded agents, twenty each, and route each request between them by keyword

architect-professional-practice-3.rationale: At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees the tools its task needs and pulls in others when required. Terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch gateway tool (C) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism, and two always-loaded halves (D) still carry twenty tools of bloat each.
architect-professional-practice-3.evidence: Large tool catalogs should be loaded on demand (tool search, deferred loading, scoped toolsets) rather than all at once.

architect-professional-practice-4.task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
architect-professional-practice-4.question: A bank wants a service that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?

options.A: One supervisor agent coordinating specialist sub-agents for both tasks, since both consume policy documents
options.B: A single agent holding retrieval and template tools, with a routing prompt choosing the behavior per request
options.C: A cited-answer retrieval service for policy questions plus a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated separately
options.D: A model fine-tuned on policy manuals and past decline letters that handles both tasks without retrieval or templates

architect-professional-practice-4.rationale: Two problems with different shapes get the two simplest reliable structures, and each can be tested and governed on its own metrics. Shared document handling is not an architectural argument for a multi-agent system (A), one agent with every tool (B) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (D) is the costliest route to problems that retrieval and templates already solve.
architect-professional-practice-4.evidence: Start with the simplest pattern that works; add agentic autonomy only when the path cannot be predetermined.

architect-professional-practice-5.task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
architect-professional-practice-5.question: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow rather than an autonomous agent for insurance claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?

options.A: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in production, so a workflow is the conservative choice until agents mature
options.B: Workflows outperform agents on accuracy for every intake task, so the board should default to them
options.C: The delivery date left no time to build and test agent tooling, so a workflow was the practical option
options.D: The intake path is known in advance, so fixed orchestration is cheaper and auditable; autonomy suits open paths

architect-professional-practice-5.rationale: The framework is structural fit: a known path gets deterministic orchestration, an open-ended path earns an agent. Novelty (A) and a universal claim of superiority (B) are not engineering arguments, and schedule pressure (C) justifies a plan, not an architecture.
architect-professional-practice-5.evidence: Use workflows for well-defined tasks needing predictability; use agents when flexibility and model-driven decisions are needed at scale.

architect-professional-practice-6.task: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
architect-professional-practice-6.question: A law firm's assistant summarizes contract clauses, and the partners disagree about whether the summaries are "good". Quality is subjective and there is no single correct summary. What makes the evaluation tractable?

options.A: Define a rubric of the failure modes counsel cares about, grade a labeled set with it, and add human review
options.B: Compare each summary with one counsel-written reference using exact or fuzzy string matching against a pass threshold
options.C: Release to a pilot group and track how many summaries lawyers edit before filing, treating edits as the quality score
options.D: Have the model rate its own summaries from one to ten and average the ratings across the clause set

architect-professional-practice-6.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through an explicit rubric, a labeled set built with domain experts, and mixed methods where humans anchor the model grader. String matching against one reference (B) fails every valid paraphrase, edit counts (C) arrive late and mix style with errors, and self-rating (D) has no calibration against human judgment.
architect-professional-practice-6.evidence: Combine code graders, rubric-based LLM grading calibrated to human labels, and human review for subjective tasks.

architect-professional-practice-7.task: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
architect-professional-practice-7.question: A rewritten system prompt for a customer-facing assistant looks better in demos to the product owner. Before rolling it out to all users, what is the disciplined path?

options.A: Review twenty demo outputs with the product owner and the support lead, and ship the change if both approve
options.B: Run the regression set, then A/B test against the current prompt on live traffic with predefined metrics
options.C: Deploy to all users behind a feature flag and compare this week's satisfaction scores with last week's
options.D: Have the team vote on blind side-by-side outputs and roll out when the new prompt wins a majority

architect-professional-practice-7.rationale: A prompt change is a production change: the regression set catches breakage, and an A/B test on predefined metrics shows real improvement before full exposure. Demo review (A) and a team vote (D) are anecdotes, and a full rollout compared with last week (C) has no concurrent control, so seasonality and traffic mix confound the result.
architect-professional-practice-7.evidence: Evaluate prompt changes against a fixed test set and compare variants on predefined success criteria before shipping.

architect-professional-practice-8.task: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
architect-professional-practice-8.question: A hospital network requires that no protected health information (PHI) reach the model provider, yet clinicians want to ask free-text questions about patients. Which design satisfies both requirements?

options.A: A policy asking clinicians not to type patient identifiers, backed by annual privacy training and attestation
options.B: A system prompt telling the model to ignore and never repeat any patient identifiers it sees in a query
options.C: A de-identification layer that tokenizes PHI before the API call, restores it locally, and is audited at the boundary
options.D: A fixed menu of pre-approved question templates so that free-text input never reaches the model at all

architect-professional-practice-8.rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, results are re-associated locally, and the control can be audited. Training and attestation (A) are not a technical control, a prompt instruction (B) acts after the data has already left, and a template menu (D) drops the free-text requirement that a compliant design can still meet.
architect-professional-practice-8.evidence: Minimize and de-identify sensitive data before it leaves the trust boundary, and keep the control auditable.

architect-professional-practice-9.task: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
architect-professional-practice-9.question: An executive sponsor demands "99.9% accuracy or we cancel" for a document-review solution. Measured task accuracy plateaus near 92%, and human reviewers catch most of the remaining errors. What is the architect's correct move?

options.A: Commit to 99.9% in the contract, relying on planned model upgrades and prompt tuning to close the gap
options.B: Report accuracy on the easiest subset of cases, where the system already exceeds 99%, as the headline figure
options.C: Tell the sponsor accuracy targets are an engineering matter and offer only latency and uptime commitments
options.D: Reframe the target as end-to-end error rate with confidence-routed human review, showing rates and costs

architect-professional-practice-9.rationale: Setting expectations with explicit, honest trade-offs is the architect's job: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (A), cherry-picking a subset (B), and refusing to discuss accuracy (C) each damage the trust the role exists to build.
architect-professional-practice-9.evidence: Align stakeholders on measurable end-to-end outcomes and be explicit about error rates, human review, and the cost trade-off.

architect-professional-practice-10.task: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
architect-professional-practice-10.question: Three product teams configure Claude Code independently. Conventions have drifted, and new engineers need days before they are productive. What is the enablement fix?

options.A: Publish a version-controlled baseline of shared configuration, skills, and commands, with team rules layered on
options.B: Document the conventions on a wiki page and ask each engineer to paste the relevant rules into a personal CLAUDE.md
options.C: Standardize on one team's configuration and copy it unchanged into every repository, with no per-team overrides allowed
options.D: Run an onboarding workshop each quarter and let engineers keep whatever local settings they have found effective

architect-professional-practice-10.rationale: Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration that teams extend locally, which scales and keeps new hires on the same footing. A wiki plus personal files (B) recreates drift, a single copied configuration with no overrides (C) ignores real differences between teams, and workshops with free-form local settings (D) are the status quo with slides.
architect-professional-practice-10.evidence: Share project CLAUDE.md, settings and skills through version control, layered with user and local scopes for personal or team differences.

architect-professional-practice-11.task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
architect-professional-practice-11.question: A pharmaceutical customer's security policy states that no request data may leave their AWS account, and procurement wants to reuse their existing AWS agreement. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?

options.A: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement and zero data retention enabled for the organization
options.B: Claude through Amazon Bedrock, invoked inside the customer's own AWS account and chosen region
options.C: The Claude API called through a customer-managed VPN tunnel with all request logging disabled on their side
options.D: The Claude API with TLS enforced end to end and customer-managed KMS keys on any stored logs

architect-professional-practice-11.rationale: A constraint that data stays inside the customer's cloud boundary is met by running Claude within that boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contract with zero retention (A), a VPN tunnel with logging off (C), and strong encryption with customer keys (D) are all protections for data that still leaves the account.
architect-professional-practice-11.evidence: Claude models are available through Amazon Bedrock, so requests run under the customer's AWS account, controls and region.

architect-professional-practice-12.task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
architect-professional-practice-12.question: An enterprise has standardized on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit for AI workloads to flow through its existing controls. How should the architect deploy Claude?

options.A: Deploy on Amazon Bedrock and federate the enterprise's identities across clouds to reuse its governance
options.B: Use the Claude API directly and rebuild identity, billing, and audit integration in the enterprise's tooling
options.C: Deploy through Vertex AI so IAM, consolidated billing, and audit logging apply without duplicate controls
options.D: Let each team pick the Claude access path that suits its workload and reconcile billing at quarter end

architect-professional-practice-12.rationale: Aligning with the cloud the enterprise already governs means its identity, billing and audit controls apply without duplication. A second cloud (A) adds another control plane, rebuilding controls on the direct API (B) is costly and drifts, and per-team choice (D) removes governance altogether.
architect-professional-practice-12.evidence: Claude is offered on Vertex AI, so Google Cloud IAM, billing and logging cover usage.

architect-professional-practice-13.task: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
architect-professional-practice-13.question: A platform team routes all application traffic to Claude through one internal gateway service instead of letting each application call the provider directly. What is the principal architectural benefit?

options.A: Token spend drops because the gateway compresses prompts and removes duplicate system content before every call
options.B: Per-application evaluation becomes unnecessary because the gateway validates output quality for every caller
options.C: End-to-end latency falls because the gateway keeps warm connections that skip the provider's normal network path
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced and changed in one place for every application

architect-professional-practice-13.rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not inherently compress prompts (A), it cannot replace each application's own evaluation (B), and an extra network hop generally adds latency rather than removing it (C).
architect-professional-practice-13.evidence: Centralizing access gives one place to apply authentication, quotas, logging and routing for all consumers.

architect-professional-practice-14.task: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
architect-professional-practice-14.question: A legacy order system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the Claude task needs several seconds of reasoning to meet its accuracy bar. What is the appropriate design?

options.A: Accept the request, return a job ID inside the timeout, and deliver the result later by callback or polling
options.B: Cap the output tokens so the response completes inside two seconds, and accept shorter, less complete answers
options.C: Negotiate a longer timeout in the legacy system's endpoint configuration at the next scheduled release train
options.D: Switch to the fastest model tier with streaming enabled so the first tokens arrive inside two seconds

architect-professional-practice-14.rationale: Decoupling submission from delivery lets the timeout constraint and the reasoning workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating output (B) and dropping to the fastest tier (D) sacrifice the accuracy bar the task needs, and changing the legacy timeout (C) targets a system whose limit is the stated constraint.
architect-professional-practice-14.evidence: Latency-bound callers need asynchronous patterns when the task's accuracy depends on longer processing.

architect-professional-practice-15.task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
architect-professional-practice-15.question: A bank must run the same Claude solution on two clouds to satisfy separate regional regulators. What is the most important design consideration?

options.A: Keep one prompt set byte-for-byte identical on both platforms, since identical inputs guarantee identical behavior
options.B: Define which behaviors must be identical across platforms, then run the evaluation suite on each deployment
options.C: Standardize on the cheaper platform's model catalog and pricing tier, and mirror that setup on the other cloud
options.D: Place each deployment in the region nearest its users and track latency as the only expected variance

architect-professional-practice-15.rationale: Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified on each deployment, not assumed. Identical prompts (A) do not guarantee identical behavior across platforms and versions, and cost (C) or proximity (D) say nothing about consistency.
architect-professional-practice-15.evidence: Verify behavior on each platform with the same evaluations; platforms can differ in available features and model versions.

architect-professional-practice-16.task: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
architect-professional-practice-16.question: A finance director asks for an autonomous agent to run the invoice-to-payment approval process end to end. What should the architect establish first?

options.A: Which Claude model tier gives the best accuracy on invoice extraction in a representative sample of documents
options.B: The expected monthly token spend for the full approval volume, so the business case can be signed off
options.C: Which approval decisions carry personal accountability or regulatory duty and must stay with a named person
options.D: Whether the agent, its integrations, and its test suite can be delivered before the quarter-end deadline

architect-professional-practice-16.rationale: Where accountability sits determines what may be automated at all and shapes the whole solution. Model choice (A), spend (B), and the delivery date (D) are all downstream of that boundary.
architect-professional-practice-16.evidence: Keep humans in the loop for consequential, irreversible or accountable decisions and design autonomy around that boundary.

architect-professional-practice-17.task: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
architect-professional-practice-17.question: Two designs for a document-intake solution both meet the functional requirement. One is simpler; the other adds an extra agent for slightly higher extraction accuracy. What should decide between them?

options.A: Choose the more capable design, because the extra accuracy lowers the long-term support burden for the team
options.B: Choose whichever design the engineering team is more excited to build, since motivation drives delivery quality
options.C: Choose the design with more components, since each added agent leaves room for future requirements
options.D: Whether a stated requirement needs the extra accuracy, weighed against the ongoing cost of operating the added agent

architect-professional-practice-17.rationale: Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it has to be bought by a stated requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), team preference (B), and speculative flexibility (C) all pay that cost without justification.
architect-professional-practice-17.evidence: Add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes; prefer the simplest solution that meets the requirement.

architect-professional-practice-18.task: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
architect-professional-practice-18.question: A proposed claims design relies on the model itself to decide when a regulator-mandated disclosure must be added to customer letters. What is the correct judgment?

options.A: Unacceptable as designed: a mandated control must be enforced by deterministic code outside the model
options.B: Acceptable if the evaluation set shows the model applies the disclosure correctly in over 99% of cases
options.C: Acceptable if the rule is written into the system prompt and disclosed to the regulator as probabilistic
options.D: Acceptable if the team upgrades to the largest model tier and adds a second model to double-check outputs

architect-professional-practice-18.rationale: A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behavior cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. High accuracy (B), a disclosure to the regulator (C), and a bigger or doubled model (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.
architect-professional-practice-18.evidence: Must-happen controls belong in code, hooks or gates outside the model; prompts are probabilistic.

architect-professional-practice-19.task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
architect-professional-practice-19.question: In a design review of a customer-service solution, which finding is the clearest sign that the solution has been over-engineered?

options.A: The solution routes different tasks to more than one Claude model tier, chosen per task by cost and quality
options.B: Components such as a planner agent and a second vector store trace to no stated requirement
options.C: The evaluation suite contains more test cases than the application has lines of prompt text, built over months
options.D: The workflow includes a human approval step before refunds above a set amount are issued

architect-professional-practice-19.rationale: Components that no requirement depends on are the definition of over-engineering and the parts that will rot. Using several model tiers (A), a thorough evaluation suite (C), and an approval step for large refunds (D) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.
architect-professional-practice-19.evidence: Find the simplest solution possible and increase complexity only when needed.

architect-professional-practice-20.task: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
architect-professional-practice-20.question: A team asks the architect to sign off that its claims-triage assistant is ready for production. What must exist before readiness can be claimed?

options.A: A stakeholder demonstration in which the assistant answered the sponsor's hand-picked questions correctly
options.B: Sign-off from the engineering team that the code is complete, reviewed, and deployed in staging
options.C: A stated success criterion and measured performance against it on data representative of production
options.D: A finished cost model showing projected spend per request and per month at the expected volume

architect-professional-practice-20.rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what separates it from an impression. A demonstration (A), engineering consensus (B), and a cost model (D) do not show whether the system works on real inputs.
architect-professional-practice-20.evidence: Define success criteria up front and measure against representative test cases before deployment.

architect-professional-practice-21.task: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
architect-professional-practice-21.question: A team builds the evaluation set for its support assistant by sampling only tickets the assistant already resolves correctly. What is the consequence?

options.A: The scores form a reliable baseline that will expose any later regression, whatever the ticket category
options.B: The set is acceptable once it exceeds a few thousand examples, because volume averages out the selection
options.C: The bias matters only for regulated systems, where auditors expect coverage of rare categories
options.D: It overstates performance and hides the failure modes, because hard and rare cases are missing from the sample

architect-professional-practice-21.rationale: An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and the failures that matter are exactly the cases left out. A baseline that cannot see them (A) is not reliable, more volume (B) does not fix a biased sample, and the problem applies to every system, not only regulated ones (C).
architect-professional-practice-21.evidence: Evaluation sets should be representative and include edge cases and past failures.

architect-professional-practice-22.task: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
architect-professional-practice-22.question: A prompt revision raised the team's target metric but silently degraded refusal behavior that nobody measures. How is this class of problem best prevented?

options.A: Keep a regression suite covering must-keep behaviors, and run it on every prompt change
options.B: Change only one sentence of the prompt per release so any regression can be traced back to its cause
options.C: Add a second reviewer to every prompt change, so that a regression is noticed before it is shipped
options.D: Limit prompt changes to a monthly release window so fewer regressions can accumulate

architect-professional-practice-22.rationale: Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break, on every change. Single-sentence changes (B) and extra reviewers (C) reduce risk without detecting anything, and a slower cadence (D) batches regressions instead of preventing them.
architect-professional-practice-22.evidence: Regression-test every prompt change against cases covering behaviors that must be preserved.

architect-professional-practice-23.task: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
architect-professional-practice-23.question: A deployed claims-summarization solution has been stable for six months. What should trigger a re-evaluation against the evaluation set?

options.A: A reported incident, because incidents are the only evidence that earlier measurements no longer hold
options.B: A change to the model, the prompt, the input data distribution, or the requirement itself
options.C: A fixed annual review date set at launch, which gives auditors a predictable evidence cycle
options.D: A change in monthly spend, since cost movement is a reliable signal that quality has moved too

architect-professional-practice-23.rationale: Any change to what determines behavior invalidates the earlier measurement, so those changes trigger re-evaluation. Waiting for incidents (A) detects problems late, a fixed calendar date (C) is unrelated to actual change, and spend (D) says little about correctness.
architect-professional-practice-23.evidence: Re-run evaluations whenever the model, prompt, data or requirements change, and monitor production for drift.

architect-professional-practice-24.task: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
architect-professional-practice-24.question: A compliance officer asks the architect to log full prompts and responses of an HR assistant for audit. Prompts may contain employee personal data. How should the architect treat the request?

options.A: Implement full logging immediately, because audit requirements override data-protection duties
options.B: Decline the request, because retaining prompts and responses creates a privacy exposure the client cannot accept
options.C: Establish what the audit must evidence, then log the minimum, protected and retained, that satisfies it
options.D: Log responses only, because prompts hold user input while responses are merely derived content

architect-professional-practice-24.rationale: Audit and data protection are both real constraints, so the design should satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket logging (A) and blanket refusal (B) each ignore one side, and a responses-only rule (D) is arbitrary and may still capture personal data.
architect-professional-practice-24.evidence: Apply data minimization, purpose limitation and retention limits while keeping the evidence trail auditors need.

architect-professional-practice-25.question: An agent summarizes inbound emails and web pages and can call internal tools to open tickets and update records. How should the architect treat content retrieved from untrusted sources?

options.A: Safe once a filter strips known injection phrases, because the remaining text can no longer carry instructions
options.B: Safe when the system prompt tells the model to ignore any instructions that appear inside retrieved text
options.C: Safe when it arrives over TLS from a domain on the company's allow-list of approved partner sites
options.D: Untrusted data throughout, so the agent's tool permissions must be bounded whatever the content persuades it to try

architect-professional-practice-25.rationale: The durable control is that the agent cannot exceed its permissions no matter what the content says, with approval for risky actions. String filters (A) and prompt instructions (B) can be bypassed, and transport security or an allow-list (C) says nothing about whether the content itself is hostile.
architect-professional-practice-25.evidence: Treat tool results and documents as untrusted data; use least-privilege tools, approvals and isolation outside the model.

architect-professional-practice-26.task: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
architect-professional-practice-26.question: An automated Claude workflow wrongly denies a customer's refund, and the customer escalates to the regulator. Who is accountable for the decision?

options.A: The deploying organization, which owns the outcomes of decisions it chose to automate
options.B: Anthropic as the model provider, since its model generated the faulty decision that the customer received
options.C: The engineer who wrote the prompt, since the prompt defined the decision logic that was applied here
options.D: No single party, since an automated decision has no human decision-maker to attribute it to

architect-professional-practice-26.rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (B) supplies a capability, individual authorship (C) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation does not dissolve accountability (D).
architect-professional-practice-26.evidence: Organizations deploying AI remain responsible for its decisions; design human oversight and transparency accordingly.

architect-professional-practice-27.question: An executive sponsor asks the architect for a single number that shows how good the new solution is. What is the right response?

options.A: Provide the headline accuracy percentage from the latest evaluation, since it is simple and comparable
options.B: Provide the one measure tied to the decision the sponsor faces, with what it does not cover stated
options.C: Explain that a language model's quality cannot be reduced to one figure and offer a dashboard instead
options.D: Provide the model's published benchmark score, since it is independently verified and widely recognized

architect-professional-practice-27.rationale: A useful metric is tied to the decision at hand and honest about its limits. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a public benchmark (D) can mislead about this workload, and refusing to summarize (C) fails the sponsor.
architect-professional-practice-27.evidence: Report metrics that map to business outcomes and be explicit about their limits and assumptions.

architect-professional-practice-28.task: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
architect-professional-practice-28.question: A pilot with ten users succeeded, and the business wants to roll the assistant out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: The cost of licenses and API spend for two thousand users compared with the budget approved for the pilot
options.B: Whether a larger model tier is needed to sustain quality across a much wider range of users
options.C: Which pilot assumptions about users, inputs, and edge cases may not hold at scale
options.D: The schedule for training the new users and publishing documentation before the wider launch

architect-professional-practice-28.rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming them is the architect's contribution before committing to a rollout. Cost (A), model size (B), and training (D) are downstream of knowing what breaks.
architect-professional-practice-28.evidence: Validate pilot assumptions against production scale and representative data before expanding.

architect-professional-practice-29.task: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
architect-professional-practice-29.question: A consultancy is handing a Claude solution to the client's operations team. What most reduces the risk that the solution decays after handover?

options.A: Comprehensive architecture documentation delivered and signed off at handover
options.B: An extended warranty obliging the vendor to fix defects for twelve months after go-live
options.C: Live training sessions for every end user during the first month after go-live
options.D: A named owner with a standing evaluation, monitoring, and update routine

architect-professional-practice-29.rationale: Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artifacts produced once. Documentation (A) and training (C) age, and a warranty (B) covers defects rather than the drift of models, data and requirements.
architect-professional-practice-29.evidence: Handoff should include owners and operating procedures for monitoring, evaluation and iteration.

architect-professional-practice-30.task: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
architect-professional-practice-30.question: A document-processing solution has three tasks: bulk classification, contract clause analysis, and drafting executive summaries. How should the architect choose models?

options.A: Pick for each task the cheapest tier that meets its quality bar on an evaluation, and re-test when models change
options.B: Standardize on a single mid-tier model for all three tasks so prompts, caching, and monitoring stay uniform
options.C: Use the most capable tier for every task, since the hardest task sets the quality requirement for the others
options.D: Use whichever model was released most recently for all tasks, since each generation beats the last on every task

architect-professional-practice-30.rationale: Different tasks have different quality bars, and matching each to the cheapest tier that passes an evaluation keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. One mid-tier model (B), the top tier everywhere (C), and the newest release (D) each choose by convenience or assumption rather than measured fit.
architect-professional-practice-30.evidence: Choose the cheapest model tier that meets the quality bar measured by an eval, and pin and re-evaluate versions.

architect-professional-practice-31.task: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
architect-professional-practice-31.question: An architect is designing a production assistant that combines instructions, retrieved documents, and conversation state. How should the context window be treated in the design?

options.A: As a capacity to fill as completely as possible, since more retrieved material gives the model more evidence
options.B: As a budget allocated deliberately among instructions, retrieved material, and working state, each share justified
options.C: As a limit that matters only when documents are long, so short-input applications need no context planning
options.D: As a setting to raise whenever answer quality drops, since quality loss usually means truncated input

architect-professional-practice-31.rationale: Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (A) invites dilution and cost, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.
architect-professional-practice-31.evidence: Treat context as a finite resource; include the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the desired behavior.

architect-professional-practice-32.task: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
architect-professional-practice-32.question: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged, so the same task now behaves differently across products. What is the appropriate remedy?

options.A: Appoint one team as sole author of every prompt, with the other teams submitting change requests by ticket
options.B: Freeze all prompts at their current versions until the three teams agree on a single standard wording
options.C: Keep prompts in version control with named owners, peer review, and an evaluation run on every change
options.D: Move every team's instructions into one shared system prompt so the behavior is defined in a single place

architect-professional-practice-32.rationale: Prompts that determine production behavior deserve the same lifecycle as code: versioning, ownership, review and tests. Centralizing authorship (A) may not fit the organization, freezing (B) blocks improvement, and one merged system prompt (D) hides conflicts instead of governing them.
architect-professional-practice-32.evidence: Manage prompts as versioned, tested artifacts with clear ownership and reuse mechanisms.

architect-professional-practice-33.task: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
architect-professional-practice-33.question: An organization with sixty repositories wants consistent Claude Code practice across them. What is the most durable approach?

options.A: A conventions policy circulated by email to engineering leads each quarter and acknowledged by each team
options.B: A recorded training session on Claude Code, attended by one champion per repository
options.C: A manager approval step required before an engineer starts each Claude Code session
options.D: A committed CLAUDE.md and shared skills in each repository, changed through pull requests like code

architect-professional-practice-33.rationale: Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work, so every session loads them automatically. Emailed policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-session approval (C) adds friction without conveying any practice.
architect-professional-practice-33.evidence: Project CLAUDE.md and skills are committed to the repo and loaded automatically for everyone working in it.

architect-professional-practice-34.task: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
architect-professional-practice-34.question: A VP asks how the organization will know whether its Claude Code enablement program is working. What is the most useful measure?

options.A: Movement in targeted outcomes such as cycle time, defect escapes, and onboarding time
options.B: The number of engineers who completed the training sessions and certified on the tooling
options.C: The share of purchased licenses that were active in a given month across the organization
options.D: The total volume of completions and tool calls generated per engineer per week across the organization

architect-professional-practice-34.rationale: Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, so that is what should be measured. Attendance (B), license utilization (C), and activity volume (D) show uptake, not benefit.
architect-professional-practice-34.evidence: Measure the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve, not just adoption activity.

architect-professional-practice-35.task: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
architect-professional-practice-35.question: A team reports that Claude Code works well on new services but produces poor changes on a ten-year-old legacy service. What should the architect investigate first?

options.A: Whether the team needs a prompting refresher, since legacy code demands more precise instructions
options.B: Whether the legacy service lacks committed context, such as a CLAUDE.md, conventions, and test commands
options.C: Whether a larger model tier would infer the legacy service's undocumented behavior without extra context
options.D: Whether the legacy service should be rewritten first so Claude Code can work with a modern structure

architect-professional-practice-35.rationale: A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each, and that context is cheap to supply. Training (A) does not supply repository context, a larger model (C) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.
architect-professional-practice-35.evidence: Claude Code relies on project memory (CLAUDE.md) and repository context to follow conventions and run the right checks.

architect-professional-mock1-1.task: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
architect-professional-mock1-1.question: A retailer wants Claude to answer shopper questions from a 40,000-document product catalog whose prices and stock change daily. Answers must reflect the previous day's changes. Which architecture fits?

options.A: Fine-tune a model on the catalog each night so product facts live in the model's weights
options.B: Give an agent a web browsing tool and let it search the retailer's public site for every question
options.C: Retrieve from an index refreshed as the catalog changes and answer from the retrieved passages
options.D: Place the full catalog in a cached system prompt and refresh the cache each morning

architect-professional-mock1-1.rationale: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window, so refreshing the index keeps answers current at modest cost. Nightly fine-tuning (A) is slow and expensive, browsing the public site (B) is unreliable and uncontrolled, and a forty-thousand-document prompt (D) exceeds practical context and cache economics.
architect-professional-mock1-1.evidence: Use retrieval to ground answers in current external knowledge instead of baking facts into the model.

architect-professional-mock1-2.task: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
architect-professional-mock1-2.question: After a catalog re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products, such as the right style in the wrong product generation. The generation prompt and model version are unchanged. Which investigation comes first?

options.A: The generation prompt, to tell the model to prefer the newest product among the retrieved items
options.B: The model version, by comparing today's answers with a snapshot taken before the re-index
options.C: The chat interface, which may be sending a truncated or reworded version of the shopper's question
options.D: Chunking and embedding settings, and whether every vector was rebuilt consistently

architect-professional-mock1-2.rationale: Degradation right after a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency, since retrieval is what returned the wrong items. Prompt wording (A) papers over a retrieval fault, the unchanged model (B) does not correlate with the re-index, and the interface (C) would not produce semantically near but wrong matches.
architect-professional-mock1-2.evidence: Retrieval quality depends on chunking, embedding and index construction; rebuilds can silently change all three.

architect-professional-mock1-3.task: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
architect-professional-mock1-3.question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems, and tool-selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?

options.A: Scope toolsets per role or task and load the rest by progressive discovery
options.B: Shorten every tool description so all 45 definitions occupy a smaller share of the context
options.C: Merge related tools into a few multi-mode tools that take an action parameter and a payload
options.D: Move to the most capable model tier so it can choose correctly among all 45 definitions

architect-professional-mock1-3.rationale: At large tool counts, scoping toolsets and loading the rest on demand preserves selection quality and trims context. Shorter descriptions (B) remove the guidance the model needs, multi-mode tools (C) move the ambiguity inside the parameters, and a bigger model (D) pays more to tolerate the same bloat.
architect-professional-mock1-3.evidence: Few well-scoped tools beat many overlapping ones; load large catalogs on demand with tool search.

architect-professional-mock1-4.task: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
architect-professional-mock1-4.question: A legal-operations team ships a summarization feature whose quality is judged subjectively by reviewers. Which evaluation design best fits?

options.A: Score each summary by exact match against one human-written reference summary for the same document
options.B: Apply a rubric of key failure modes with model graders, calibrated by periodic audits on a human-labeled set
options.C: Compare each summary's length with the reference length and flag anything outside a tolerance band
options.D: Rely on user thumbs-up and thumbs-down counts from production as the only quality signal

architect-professional-mock1-4.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the grader. Exact match (A) rejects valid paraphrases, length comparison (C) measures size rather than quality, and thumbs counts alone (D) are sparse, biased, and arrive after release.
architect-professional-mock1-4.evidence: Use LLM-as-judge with a rubric calibrated against human labels, with human review for subtle cases.

architect-professional-mock1-5.task: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
architect-professional-mock1-5.question: A fraud-triage team wants to ship a revised prompt to all analysts this week. What is the disciplined sequence before it reaches everyone?

options.A: Ship it and watch the support queue for complaints during the first week of operation
options.B: Hold a team vote on side-by-side samples, then roll out to all users if the new prompt wins
options.C: Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B on predefined metrics, then rollout
options.D: Roll out to all analysts with an in-product feedback form and revert if ratings fall noticeably

architect-professional-mock1-5.rationale: Prompt changes are production changes: regression evaluation first, then a controlled comparison on predefined metrics, then rollout. Complaint-watching (A) and a feedback form with rollback (D) test on everyone with no control, and a vote (B) is opinion rather than measurement.
architect-professional-mock1-5.evidence: Compare prompt variants against the current one on predefined metrics, and regression-test before release.

architect-professional-mock1-6.task: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
architect-professional-mock1-6.question: A hospital network's compliance office has ruled that protected health information may not be sent to any model provider, yet clinicians need free-text search over notes that contain patient names and record numbers. Which design meets both requirements?

options.A: Sign a business associate agreement with the provider and send notes unchanged, since the contract covers the disclosure
options.B: Instruct the model in the system prompt to ignore and never repeat any identifiers found in the clinical notes it receives
options.C: Limit search to structured fields such as diagnosis codes and drop free-text queries, since notes cannot be protected
options.D: Tokenize identifiers in a local de-identification step before the call, re-attach them locally afterward, and audit every substitution

architect-professional-mock1-6.rationale: A boundary that says PHI must not reach the provider is satisfied only by an architectural control that strips identifiers before data crosses it, with re-association kept on the hospital side and an audit trail, which is what (D) does. A contract (A) permits the disclosure the office prohibited. A prompt instruction (B) acts after the data has already been sent. Dropping free text (C) fails the clinicians' stated need.
architect-professional-mock1-6.evidence: Compliance boundaries are enforced by controlling what data crosses to the model; de-identification with local re-linking keeps sensitive data inside the customer's environment.

architect-professional-mock1-7.question: A claims assistant handles about 40,000 claims a month, and the six-person review team can read roughly 2,000. Leadership wants human review to prevent costly mistakes without hiring more staff. Which review policy fits?

options.A: Send claims to reviewers when confidence is low or the payout is high, and let routine low-value claims proceed automatically
options.B: Review a uniform random 5% of all claims so reviewers see an unbiased picture of every claim type the system handles
options.C: Let every claim pay out first, then have reviewers audit batches afterward and reverse any payments found to be wrong
options.D: Review only the claims the claimant disputes, since disputes surface the real errors without spending reviewer time on other claims

architect-professional-mock1-7.rationale: Review capacity is scarce, so it should go where error likelihood and consequence are highest: (A) routes by confidence and impact. Uniform sampling (B) spends most reviews on routine cases and misses most high-impact errors. Post-payout audits (C) detect harm after it happens. Dispute-driven review (D) only catches errors claimants notice and challenge.
architect-professional-mock1-7.evidence: Human oversight is most effective when concentrated at checkpoints where risk and uncertainty are highest, rather than applied uniformly.

architect-professional-mock1-8.question: A VP sponsoring a contract-extraction project asks for one accuracy number for the board deck. Your evaluation shows 97% on typed invoices but 71% on handwritten scans, which are 20% of volume and are checked by staff before filing. What should you present?

options.A: Present the 97% invoice figure, and note that handwritten scans will be improved in a later phase of the delivery roadmap
options.B: Report results per document type with the blended figure, how it was measured, and the outcome after human review
options.C: Give the blended figure alone, rounded to a whole number, and place the per-type breakdown in an appendix for anyone who asks
options.D: Decline to give any number until scan accuracy has been raised to the same level as the invoice accuracy

architect-professional-mock1-8.rationale: A single headline number hides the segment that carries the risk, so the architect should show the breakdown with method and the end-to-end result after review, as (B) does. Quoting only the best segment (A) misleads. A blended figure buried in an appendix (C) hides the variation from the decision-makers. Refusing to quantify (D) withholds information the sponsor needs.
architect-professional-mock1-8.evidence: Evaluation results should be reported against defined success criteria and broken out by task type so stakeholders can see where performance differs.

architect-professional-mock1-9.task: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
architect-professional-mock1-9.question: A retailer is deploying a support assistant that will see EU customers' order history and messages. Counsel asks which GDPR-derived requirements should shape the architecture itself, beyond the contract. Which should the architect prioritize?

options.A: Selecting a model provider headquartered in the EU, so that no transfer analysis is needed for any of the customer data
options.B: Encrypting stored conversations at rest, which on its own satisfies the regulation's obligations for any personal data held
options.C: Collecting only needed data, using it for the stated purpose, and being able to locate and erase one person's data
options.D: Recording a consent checkbox at account creation, which then covers every later processing purpose the retailer may add

architect-professional-mock1-9.rationale: Data protection principles translate into design: collect minimally, bind use to a stated purpose, and support erasure on request, as in (C). Provider location (A) does not remove the need to analyze transfers and processing. Encryption (B) protects confidentiality but not minimization, purpose, or erasure. A one-time consent box (D) does not cover new purposes.
architect-professional-mock1-9.evidence: Minimization, purpose limitation and erasure are design-level data-protection requirements that must be supported by how data is collected, stored and deleted.

architect-professional-mock1-10.task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
architect-professional-mock1-10.question: An insurer's document intake always runs the same steps: classify, extract fields, validate against policy rules, then file. A vendor proposes a fully autonomous agent for flexibility. What is the strongest reason to prefer a workflow here?

options.A: Workflows yield more accurate field extraction than an agent that uses the same model and the same prompts
options.B: Agents lack the tool-calling support needed to read PDF files and write records to a filing system
options.C: A workflow consumes no model context for sequencing, so each document costs less than under an agent
options.D: The path is known in advance, so fixed orchestration is cheaper, easier to test, and gives a reproducible audit trail

architect-professional-mock1-10.rationale: Autonomy earns its complexity only when the path cannot be predicted. With fixed steps, code-orchestrated sequencing is cheaper, testable, and auditable, which is (D). Accuracy depends on prompts and model, not the pattern (A). Agents can call tools (B). The model still uses context in each workflow step (C).
architect-professional-mock1-10.evidence: Use workflows for well-defined tasks needing predictability and consistency; use agents only when flexibility and model-driven decisions are needed at scale.

architect-professional-mock1-11.task: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
architect-professional-mock1-11.question: A benefits-advisor app prepends the same 12,000-token policy preamble to every request, followed by the employee's question. Both latency and input cost are over budget. Which change addresses both?

options.A: Place the preamble first, keep the volatile question after it, and mark the preamble as a prompt-cache breakpoint
options.B: Split the preamble across two sequential calls so that each request carries only half of the repeated tokens at a time
options.C: Have the model summarize the preamble at request time and send only that summary with each question
options.D: Move the preamble into a few-shot example block so the model treats it as learned behavior, not input

architect-professional-mock1-11.rationale: Prompt caching reuses a stable prefix, which cuts time to first token and the price of repeated input together; the static text must come first and the changing question after it (A). Splitting (B) adds a round trip and still resends tokens. Summarizing at request time (C) adds a model call and loses policy detail. Few-shot framing (D) does not reduce tokens sent.
architect-professional-mock1-11.evidence: Prompt caching reuses a cached prompt prefix across requests, reducing latency and cost for repeated content placed at the start of the prompt.

architect-professional-mock1-12.task: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
architect-professional-mock1-12.question: A new architect joins a Claude-based claims platform and asks why the team chose a retrieval workflow over an agent. Nobody can remember the reasoning. What should the team's architecture decision records have captured?

options.A: The final component diagram showing the chosen design, versioned alongside the application source code and tests
options.B: The decision, the alternatives rejected, the trade-offs weighed, and the constraints that drove the choice
options.C: The timeline, the owners, and the sign-off dates, so each decision can be traced to the people who approved it
options.D: The prompts and model versions in use when the decision was made, for reproducing behavior

architect-professional-mock1-12.rationale: A decision record exists to preserve the reasoning: what was chosen, what else was considered, what was traded off, and which constraints decided it (B). A diagram (A) shows the outcome but not why. Dates and owners (C) show who and when, not why. Prompts and versions (D) support reproducibility, not rationale.
architect-professional-mock1-12.evidence: Design guidance should record the trade-offs between simpler and more complex patterns so that added complexity is justified by requirements.

architect-professional-mock1-13.task: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
architect-professional-mock1-13.question: A production support agent intermittently refunds the wrong order. The logs hold only the final answer and p95 latency, so the team cannot tell whether retrieval, a tool call, or the model's reasoning failed. What should be captured?

options.A: Full text of every user message and final answer, retained for ninety days so that incidents can be replayed
options.B: Per-tool latency and error-rate dashboards, broken down by endpoint and refreshed every minute across regions
options.C: Per-request traces linking each tool call, retrieved context, and decision point to the final output
options.D: A thumbs-up or thumbs-down rating with free-text comments, gathered at the end of every support session

architect-professional-mock1-13.rationale: To localize a failure to retrieval, a tool, or the model, each step must be visible: traces connecting tool calls, retrieved context, and decisions to the output (C). Inputs and outputs alone (A) hide the intermediate steps. Per-tool latency and error rates (B) show health, not whether a wrong order was selected. User ratings (D) show that something went wrong, not where.
architect-professional-mock1-13.evidence: Agent evaluation and debugging rely on transcripts and traces of every step so failures can be attributed to a specific layer.

architect-professional-mock1-14.task: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
architect-professional-mock1-14.question: A partner business unit wants to adopt your Claude Code setup after seeing a demo. A similar handoff last year faded within a quarter as engineers drifted back to defaults. What makes adoption durable this time?

options.A: A recorded walkthrough of the workflow plus a written FAQ stored in the partner team's wiki
options.B: A dedicated chat channel where members of the original team answer questions as they arise
options.C: One-to-one coaching for each engineer during the first two weeks, tailored to their individual habits and current projects
options.D: Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and a defined onboarding path for new engineers

architect-professional-mock1-14.rationale: Durable adoption comes from setup that travels with the repository and a path that new joiners follow: versioned shared configuration, common skills and commands, and onboarding (D). Recordings and FAQs (A) go stale, a support channel (B) depends on the original team staying available, and coaching (C) helps only the people coached.
architect-professional-mock1-14.evidence: Project memory and shared configuration committed to the repository give every team member the same conventions, commands and context.

architect-professional-mock1-15.task: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
architect-professional-mock1-15.question: An operations agent can query and update production customer records through one database credential. An audit finding says a single mistaken tool call could alter thousands of rows. Which change best reduces the risk?

options.A: Split read from write into scoped tools, limit write to roles that need it, and gate writes on approval
options.B: Write every modification to an append-only log that an engineer reviews each morning for unexpected or unauthorized changes
options.C: Add a section to the system prompt explaining that record changes are sensitive and must be double-checked first
options.D: Restrict the agent to business hours so engineers can catch any mistaken changes quickly

architect-professional-mock1-15.rationale: Least privilege shrinks what a mistake can do: separate read and write capabilities, scope write access, and gate writes on approval (A). A morning log review (B) detects damage after it occurs. A cautionary prompt (C) is probabilistic and does not limit the credential. Business-hours operation (D) changes timing, not blast radius.
architect-professional-mock1-15.evidence: Grant agents the minimum permissions needed and require approval for risky actions; permission rules enforce limits outside the model.

architect-professional-mock2-1.task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
architect-professional-mock2-1.question: A bank's policy says all inference must run inside its own AWS account and approved region, under its existing network controls. Which deployment option does this requirement point to?

options.A: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement and a zero data retention arrangement in place
options.B: The Claude API reached over a private network link from the bank's virtual private cloud
options.C: Amazon Bedrock, invoked from the bank's own AWS account in the approved region
options.D: Vertex AI, in a Google Cloud region geographically close to the bank's primary data center

architect-professional-mock2-1.rationale: The requirement is about where inference runs and under whose controls, so the model must be consumed through the cloud service in the bank's own account and region, which is (C). A contract and retention terms (A) do not move processing into the account. A private link to the vendor API (B) still sends traffic to a service outside the account. Vertex AI (D) is a different cloud.
architect-professional-mock2-1.evidence: Claude models are available through Amazon Bedrock, running within the customer's AWS account and chosen region under AWS controls.

architect-professional-mock2-2.task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
architect-professional-mock2-2.question: A manufacturer standardized on Google Cloud requires identity, billing, and audit for any AI service to flow through its existing IAM, committed-spend agreement, and audit logs. How should Claude be deployed?

options.A: Through Vertex AI, so existing identity, billing, and audit controls apply without rebuilding them
options.B: Through the Claude API directly, then build matching identity and audit controls inside an internal gateway
options.C: Through Amazon Bedrock, because its feature set is the closest match to the direct Claude API
options.D: Through whichever channel each product team prefers, governed by a shared policy document

architect-professional-mock2-2.rationale: When the organization's controls already live on a given cloud, using the model through that platform reuses them: Vertex AI for a Google Cloud shop (A). Direct API access with a rebuilt gateway (B) duplicates controls and risks drift. Bedrock (C) adds a second control plane. Team-by-team choice (D) removes central governance.
architect-professional-mock2-2.evidence: Claude is offered through Vertex AI on Google Cloud, so organizations can use their existing Google Cloud identity, billing and audit tooling.

architect-professional-mock2-3.task: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
architect-professional-mock2-3.question: Seven product teams each call the Claude API with their own keys, and the platform lead proposes one internal gateway for all model traffic. Security asks what the main architectural benefit is.

options.A: Pooling volume under one key lets the company negotiate lower unit token prices with the provider
options.B: Teams no longer need their own evaluation suites, because the gateway validates every output centrally for correctness
options.C: Every call becomes faster, since requests skip per-team connection setup and share one warm connection to the provider
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing are enforced and changed in one place for all teams

architect-professional-mock2-3.rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting controls such as authentication, rate limits, logging, and routing are applied consistently and updated once (D). A gateway does not change list pricing (A), cannot replace per-use-case evaluation (B), and adds a hop rather than guaranteeing speed (C).
architect-professional-mock2-3.evidence: Central enforcement of credentials, limits and logging reduces scattered keys and makes controls consistent across applications.

architect-professional-mock2-4.task: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
architect-professional-mock2-4.question: Two designs for an HR-policy Q&A assistant both meet the accuracy and latency targets. One is retrieval plus a single model call; the other adds a planner agent and three specialist subagents. What should decide between them?

options.A: The design with more headroom, since later requirements are likely to be harder than the current ones are
options.B: Whether any stated requirement needs the added capability, against the ongoing cost of maintaining it
options.C: The design the team finds more interesting to build, since motivation affects delivery quality and speed on the project
options.D: The design whose model ranks higher on public benchmarks, since that predicts accuracy on HR questions in particular

architect-professional-mock2-4.rationale: Complexity is paid for continuously, so it must be bought by a real requirement; the simpler design wins unless a stated need demands the extra capability, which is (B). Speculative headroom (A), team preference (C), and generic benchmark rank (D) are not tied to any requirement the client has.
architect-professional-mock2-4.evidence: Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes against requirements.

architect-professional-mock2-5.task: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
architect-professional-mock2-5.question: A payments client's compliance control says refunds above $500 need two approvers. The design relies on the model to notice the amount and request approval; testing shows 99.4% compliance. Is this acceptable?

options.A: Yes, once the 0.6% of misses are logged and reviewed every week as a documented residual risk accepted by compliance
options.B: No, enforce the threshold in code outside the model; a mandatory control needs a guarantee, not a high rate
options.C: Yes, if the system prompt is strengthened and the workload moves to a larger model tier
options.D: No, unless measured compliance reaches 99.9% on a larger evaluation set drawn from production

architect-professional-mock2-5.rationale: A control that must hold has to be enforced deterministically outside the model, in code or a gate the model cannot bypass (B). Documenting residual risk (A), strengthening the prompt or enlarging the model (C), and demanding a higher measured rate (D) all still leave a probabilistic tendency standing in for a guarantee.
architect-professional-mock2-5.evidence: Rules that must always hold should be enforced by deterministic permission rules or hooks outside the model, not by prompting alone.

architect-professional-mock2-6.task: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
architect-professional-mock2-6.question: A lender wants Claude to automate loan-eligibility decisions end to end. Testing is strong, but the regulator expects a named person to be accountable for each adverse decision. Where should the automation boundary sit?

options.A: At the level where offline testing shows the model matching experienced underwriters on past decisions
options.B: At the volume the operations team can staff for review, with everything above that automated
options.C: At the scope the business sponsor requested in the original statement of work for the project
options.D: Where accountability for the decision sits, so adverse decisions stay with a named person using Claude's output

architect-professional-mock2-6.rationale: Accountability decides what may be automated at all, and it is an architectural boundary: adverse decisions stay with a person who owns them (D). Test performance (A), staffing capacity (B), and the original scope statement (C) do not answer who is responsible for the outcome.
architect-professional-mock2-6.evidence: Autonomy suits tasks where errors are recoverable and oversight is possible; consequential decisions need human checkpoints.

architect-professional-mock2-7.task: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
architect-professional-mock2-7.question: A retailer's returns-triage assistant impressed executives in a live demo, and the sponsor wants to go live next Monday. What evidence must exist before it is declared ready for production?

options.A: A stated success criterion and measured results against it on real, representative traffic
options.B: A signed-off cost model showing the run cost per ticket compared with the current manual process, month by month
options.C: A clean run of the demo script in the production environment, witnessed by the executive sponsor
options.D: Approval from the engineering lead and the security reviewer, recorded in the release ticket before launch

architect-professional-mock2-7.rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar on realistic data (A). A cost model (B), a repeated demo (C), and recorded approvals (D) may all be needed for launch but none shows whether the assistant performs well enough on real returns.
architect-professional-mock2-7.evidence: Define success criteria first, then build evaluations that measure performance against them on representative cases.

architect-professional-mock2-8.task: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
architect-professional-mock2-8.question: An eval set for a loan-document classifier was built from 3,000 tickets the current system already resolves correctly. Scores sit at 98%, and the team wants to use the set to approve a prompt change. What is the effect of how the set was built?

options.A: It gives a conservative estimate, because easy cases make regressions easier to detect in later runs
options.B: It is harmless at 3,000 cases, because a large sample washes out any selection effects in how it was built
options.C: It overstates quality and hides the failure types that matter, since it does not reflect real traffic
options.D: It matters only in regulated domains, where auditors examine sampling

architect-professional-mock2-8.rationale: A set made only of cases the system already handles measures the wrong distribution, so it inflates scores and hides the hard cases that would reveal regressions (C). Size does not repair selection bias (B), easy cases do not make regression detection stricter (A), and the problem applies in every domain (D).
architect-professional-mock2-8.evidence: Evaluation sets should be representative and include edge cases and past failures, not only cases already handled well.

architect-professional-mock2-9.question: A bank's internal auditors ask that every prompt and response from a customer-facing assistant be logged indefinitely. Privacy counsel notes that conversations contain account details. How should the architect respond?

options.A: Implement full logging as requested, because audit requirements take precedence over privacy concerns in a regulated bank
options.B: Decline logging of prompts and responses and rely on aggregate metrics, since stored conversations are a liability
options.C: Log responses only, because prompts carry the customer's personal data while responses do not carry any
options.D: Establish what the audit actually requires, then log to meet that purpose with limited access and bounded retention

architect-professional-mock2-9.rationale: Audit and data protection are both real, so the design should serve the audit purpose without keeping more than is warranted, using scoped access and defined retention (D). Blanket logging (A) and refusal (B) each ignore one side. Splitting prompts from responses (C) is arbitrary, since responses can echo personal data.
architect-professional-mock2-9.evidence: Logging for audit should be balanced against data minimization: define the purpose, restrict access and limit how long conversation data is kept.

architect-professional-mock2-10.task: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
architect-professional-mock2-10.question: An automated Claude workflow at an insurer wrongly denies a batch of claims. The vendor terms disclaim liability, and the engineer who wrote the prompt has since left. Who is accountable?

options.A: Anthropic, as the provider whose model generated the incorrect decisions across the whole affected batch
options.B: The engineer who wrote the prompt, as the author of the faulty instructions the workflow ran on
options.C: The insurer that deployed the workflow, which owns the outcomes of decisions it automates
options.D: No one in particular, since an automated process rather than a person made the decision

architect-professional-mock2-10.rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, so the insurer is accountable (C). The provider (A) supplies a capability, one engineer's authorship (B) does not transfer organizational responsibility, and automation (D) does not remove accountability.
architect-professional-mock2-10.evidence: Organizations that deploy AI systems remain responsible for how outputs are used in decisions that affect people.

architect-professional-mock2-11.task: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
architect-professional-mock2-11.question: A COO asks for one number showing whether the new claims-summarization tool is working. Adjusters care about time saved per claim, while legal cares about missed exclusions. What is the right response?

options.A: Give the headline accuracy figure from the evaluation, since it is the standard indicator of quality
options.B: Give the metric tied to the decision she must make, and state plainly what that metric leaves out
options.C: Explain that quality has several dimensions and cannot responsibly be reduced to one figure
options.D: Give the model's published benchmark score, since an independent source validates it for the whole industry

architect-professional-mock2-11.rationale: A useful single number matches the decision the sponsor faces and is candid about its limits (B). A bare accuracy figure (A) and a generic benchmark (D) can mislead about this workflow, and refusing to reduce the answer (C) fails a sponsor who needs something actionable.
architect-professional-mock2-11.evidence: Choose metrics that reflect the business outcome and the risks that matter, and communicate what each metric does and does not measure.

architect-professional-mock2-12.task: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
