architect-professional-mock2-12.question: A ten-user legal-research pilot has gone well, and leadership wants it open to 2,000 staff next quarter. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: Which assumptions held with ten users that may break at 2,000, such as input variety, support load, and edge cases
options.B: The license and token budget at 2,000 users, with a month-by-month spending forecast
options.C: Whether a larger model tier is needed to cope with the wider range of questions
options.D: The training and rollout plan, including named champions in each department

architect-professional-mock2-12.rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, so surfacing them is the architect's first contribution (A). Budget (B), model tier (C), and training (D) are follow-on questions that can only be answered once it is known what changes at 2,000 users.
architect-professional-mock2-12.evidence: Pilot results should be validated against the broader distribution of inputs and use before scaling to a wider population.

architect-professional-mock2-13.task: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
architect-professional-mock2-13.question: An insurance solution does intake classification, policy-clause lookup, and drafting of customer letters. The team wants a single model decision for the whole system. How should models be chosen?

options.A: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its measured bar, and confirm each choice with evals
options.B: Use one mid-tier model across all tasks, to simplify pinning, monitoring, and prompt maintenance
options.C: Use the largest tier everywhere, so the hardest task sets the quality floor for all the others as well
options.D: Use the newest release everywhere, since it will also be the best choice for the simple tasks

architect-professional-mock2-13.rationale: Tasks differ in difficulty, so each should get the cheapest model that clears its own evaluated bar (A). A single uniform choice of mid-tier (B), largest (C), or newest (D) optimizes for convenience or perceived safety rather than fit, and costs more or risks quality somewhere.
architect-professional-mock2-13.evidence: Models differ in capability, speed and cost; choose the one that meets the quality bar for each task, validated by evaluation.

architect-professional-mock2-14.task: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
architect-professional-mock2-14.question: A contract-review assistant's quality fell as features were added and every request began carrying all retrieved clauses, the full playbook, and the complete chat history, nearly filling the window. How should the context window be treated in the design?

options.A: As capacity to fill, since more material gives the model more evidence to reason from
options.B: As a budget allocated on purpose among instructions, retrieved material, and working state, keeping only what the task needs
options.C: As a concern only for very long documents, not for chat-style interactions like this one
options.D: As a setting to raise to the maximum whenever answers degrade, until quality recovers

architect-professional-mock2-14.rationale: Context is a limited resource whose allocation affects quality, so it should be budgeted deliberately across instructions, retrieval, and working state (B). Filling it (A) dilutes relevant content, it matters beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix poor allocation.
architect-professional-mock2-14.evidence: Context is a finite resource; more tokens do not always improve results, so curate what goes into the window.

architect-professional-mock2-15.task: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
architect-professional-mock2-15.question: A bank with 60 repositories wants consistent Claude Code practice across its engineering teams. Which approach is most durable?

options.A: A policy memo signed by engineering leadership and reissued each quarter to every repository owner and team lead
options.B: A mandatory training session with a completion certificate for every engineer, repeated each year with refresher content
options.C: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like any other code change
options.D: A central approval step before any engineer may start a Claude Code session in a repository

architect-professional-mock2-15.rationale: Conventions persist when they live in the repository and are reviewed like code: project memory and shared skills (C). Memos (A) and one-off training (B) fade, and per-session approval (D) adds friction without conveying how to work well.
architect-professional-mock2-15.evidence: Project CLAUDE.md files committed to the repo and shared skills give consistent context to everyone who works in it.

architect-professional-mock3-1.task: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
architect-professional-mock3-1.question: A healthcare client's auditor will not accept any solution whose behavior cannot be explained for a given decision. What does this requirement constrain most?

options.A: The model selection, since only the largest tier can produce explanations an auditor will accept
options.B: The deployment region, which must match the auditor's jurisdiction so records are admissible
options.C: The architecture, which must make each decision traceable and its controls inspectable
options.D: The cost model, which must budget for external audit support each release

architect-professional-mock3-1.rationale: Explainability to an auditor is a property of the whole system: decisions must be traceable and controls inspectable by design (C). Picking a larger model (A), a region (B), or a budget line (D) does not by itself make a given decision explicable.
architect-professional-mock3-1.evidence: Recording full traces of each step makes it possible to explain and review how an agent reached a particular outcome.

architect-professional-mock3-2.task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
architect-professional-mock3-2.question: A team calls one cloud's model service directly from fifty places in application code, with no wrapper. The CTO asks what the main architectural risk is.

options.A: Changing provider or access path later becomes expensive, because the coupling reaches into application code
options.B: Token costs will run higher, because direct calls skip the volume pricing that a shared gateway can negotiate for the company
options.C: Accuracy will be lower, since models hosted on a cloud service lag behind the direct API
options.D: Responses will be slower, since each call passes through the cloud provider's shared endpoint

architect-professional-mock3-2.rationale: Coupling sets the cost of change, which is the architectural concern: with fifty direct call sites, switching provider or path means touching application code (A). The coupling itself does not raise token prices (B), lower accuracy (C), or slow responses (D).
architect-professional-mock3-2.evidence: Keep integrations simple and transparent, and avoid framework or vendor abstractions that obscure the underlying calls only when they are not needed.

architect-professional-mock3-3.task: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
architect-professional-mock3-3.question: A SaaS vendor serves users in the EU and in a country whose law requires its citizens' data to stay in-country. Latency to either region is acceptable. What follows?

options.A: One deployment in the cheaper region, with application-layer encryption of all stored records
options.B: A single global deployment, with TLS and customer-managed keys protecting data in transit
options.C: One deployment in the region with the lowest combined latency for both user groups
options.D: Separate regional deployments in which each region's data is stored and processed only inside its boundary

architect-professional-mock3-3.rationale: Residency is satisfied by keeping data within each legal boundary, which means separate regional deployments (D). Encryption (A) and (B) protect data but do not keep it in-country, and optimizing for latency (C) addresses neither rule.
architect-professional-mock3-3.evidence: Cloud deployments let customers choose the region where models run so that data stays within required geographic boundaries.

architect-professional-mock3-4.task: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
architect-professional-mock3-4.question: A client's requirements say only: make the claim-triage assistant as accurate as possible. The budget is fixed and the pilot starts in six weeks. What should the architect do first?

options.A: Choose the largest model tier and tune prompts until gains flatten, then report the ceiling reached
options.B: Establish the accuracy the use case needs and what each error costs, as a testable target
options.C: Design the most capable architecture the budget allows, then let the pilot reveal the right level
options.D: Accept the wording and define the target once the pilot has produced real data from live users

architect-professional-mock3-4.rationale: An unbounded requirement cannot be designed against or verified, so it must be turned into a target based on the needed accuracy and the cost of errors (B). Maximizing capability (A) or architecture (C) spends without a target, and deferring the target (D) leaves the pilot unanchored.
architect-professional-mock3-4.evidence: Define specific, measurable success criteria tied to the use case before building and evaluating a solution.

architect-professional-mock3-5.task: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
architect-professional-mock3-5.question: In a multi-step mortgage workflow, an extraction component and a validation component each pass their own tests, yet intermittent failures occur when records move between them; rare null values appear in the hand-off. What does this suggest?

options.A: The extraction component's model tier is too small and should be upgraded
options.B: The contract between them is underspecified, especially for missing values and error cases
options.C: A third component should be added to reconcile what the other two produce
options.D: The failures are transient, so retry with exponential backoff at the boundary will absorb them reliably

architect-professional-mock3-5.rationale: Failures at the boundary between components that each work alone point at the interface contract, especially for missing values and errors (B). A bigger model (A) and an extra reconciler (C) do not define the interface, and retries (D) mask a deterministic gap.
architect-professional-mock3-5.evidence: Reliable multi-step systems depend on clearly defined interfaces and gates between steps, with checks at each hand-off.

architect-professional-mock3-6.task: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
architect-professional-mock3-6.question: A design for an HR assistant proposes storing every model interaction indefinitely in case it is needed. The interactions include health and grievance details. What should the architect raise?

options.A: That the transcripts should be encrypted with customer-managed keys, which resolves the exposure
options.B: That growth in stored volume will make the retention bucket costly after the second year
options.C: That indexing years of transcripts will slow retrieval and degrade response times
options.D: Why the data is needed, for how long, and what obligations holding it creates

architect-professional-mock3-6.rationale: Retention creates obligations and risk, so purpose and duration must justify it before storage is designed (D). Encryption (A) protects confidentiality but not purpose or duration, and storage cost (B) and speed (C) are secondary to whether the data should be kept.
architect-professional-mock3-6.evidence: Data should be retained only as long as needed for a defined purpose, with retention periods and deletion built into the design.

architect-professional-mock3-7.task: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
architect-professional-mock3-7.question: A tax-advice assistant sometimes states a wrong deduction with high confidence, and the errors cost customers penalties. How should the design handle confident-but-wrong outputs?

options.A: Verify consequential outputs against an independent source, such as rules or reference data
options.B: Escalate only answers where the model reports low confidence, and release the rest directly to the customer
options.C: Add a second pass in which the same model critiques its own answer before the customer sees the final text
options.D: Run two different models and release only answers on which both of them agree

architect-professional-mock3-7.rationale: Independent verification is what catches confident error: check consequential outputs against rules or reference data (A). Stated confidence (B) is not evidence of correctness, self-critique (C) is not independent, and two models can agree and both be wrong (D).
architect-professional-mock3-7.evidence: Reduce hallucination risk by grounding answers in provided sources and verifying claims against them.

architect-professional-mock3-8.task: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
architect-professional-mock3-8.question: A pilot of a contract-clause extractor reports 94% accuracy, and the sponsor wants a go or no-go decision. What else must be known before the number is actionable?

options.A: How the score compares with the published benchmark for the model version in use today
options.B: Whether the score held across three consecutive runs, to rule out run-to-run variance
options.C: What the 6% of failures look like, and what each failure type costs the business
options.D: How long the evaluation took and how much compute it consumed, to budget the next round

architect-professional-mock3-8.rationale: A headline rate means little without the shape and cost of its failures: which errors occur and what each one costs (C). Benchmark comparison (A), run-to-run variance (B), and evaluation time or compute (D) do not describe the risk of deploying.
architect-professional-mock3-8.evidence: Aggregate scores need error analysis: read the failing cases to see their nature and impact before acting on a metric.

architect-professional-mock3-9.task: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
architect-professional-mock3-9.question: The provider announces a newer snapshot of the model your claims solution is pinned to, with the current one deprecated in three months. What should happen before the new version reaches production traffic?

options.A: Switch on the announcement, since successor snapshots are designed to be backward compatible with prior behavior
options.B: Switch immediately and watch dashboards more closely for a week, rolling back if metrics dip
options.C: Wait until the deprecation date, so that other customers surface any regressions first
options.D: Re-run the evaluation suite on the new version and compare it with the baseline before switching

architect-professional-mock3-9.rationale: A change to what determines behavior invalidates earlier measurements, so the suite must be re-run and compared with the baseline before production sees it (D). Assuming compatibility (A) is unsafe, and switching then monitoring (B) or waiting passively (C) either detects problems after users are affected or skips testing entirely.
architect-professional-mock3-9.evidence: Migrating to a new model version requires testing and evaluating behavior on your own use case before moving traffic.

architect-professional-mock3-10.task: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
architect-professional-mock3-10.question: A product VP asks why the loan-review solution cannot simply be fully automated, since pilot accuracy looks good. What is the most useful answer?

options.A: The technology is not mature enough yet, and revisiting the question in a year or so would be sensible
options.B: Fully automated systems of this kind carry unacceptable risk, and human review is the industry norm for lending
options.C: Name the decisions that carry accountability or can't be verified, and the risk of automating them
options.D: The budget covers a review team but not the engineering that full automation would need to be reliable

architect-professional-mock3-10.rationale: A specific, reasoned boundary is actionable and can be revisited as evidence changes: naming the decisions that carry accountability or cannot be verified (C). Generic claims about maturity (A) or risk (B) give the VP nothing to act on, and budget (D) is not the real reason.
architect-professional-mock3-10.evidence: Explain trade-offs in terms of the specific tasks where autonomy raises cost or error risk, and where human checkpoints are required.

architect-professional-mock3-11.task: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
architect-professional-mock3-11.question: A consultancy is handing a document-processing solution to the client's IT team, who will own it for a year without the original builders. What should be handed over so the solution survives?

options.A: The repository with full source code and deployment scripts, plus a runbook for redeploying
options.B: The evaluation suite, the success criteria, a named owner, and a routine for re-checking performance
options.C: A recorded demonstration of the system and a walkthrough of the architecture diagram
options.D: The final prompts and the list of model settings, with comments explaining each choice

architect-professional-mock3-11.rationale: Continuity depends on being able to measure and maintain the system with someone responsible: evaluations, criteria, an owner, and a re-check routine (B). Code and runbooks (A), demos (C), and prompts (D) are artifacts without the means to verify they still work.
architect-professional-mock3-11.evidence: Maintain evaluation suites and success criteria over time so changes to prompts, models or data can be checked for regressions.

architect-professional-mock3-12.task: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
architect-professional-mock3-12.question: A support team reports that their Claude-based summarizer has become noticeably worse over two months. The model ID is pinned, and no deploys or prompt edits occurred. What is the most likely explanation to check first?

options.A: The inputs or usage changed, such as new ticket types or longer threads
options.B: The pinned model was quietly degraded by the provider as load on it grew over the period
options.C: The prompts lose effectiveness with age and need periodic rewording to stay sharp
options.D: The original evaluation was flawed, so earlier quality was never as good as reported

architect-professional-mock3-12.rationale: Behavior changes with what is fed to it, and drift in inputs or usage is the usual cause when nothing was deployed (A). Pinned snapshots do not change underneath you (B), prompts do not wear out (C), and doubting the original evaluation (D) is not the first suspect.
architect-professional-mock3-12.evidence: Pinned model snapshots are fixed, so behavior changes in production usually come from changes in inputs, data or surrounding configuration.

architect-professional-mock3-13.task: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
architect-professional-mock3-13.question: A bank's customer-chat assistant is steered by a 3,000-word system prompt. Two incidents were traced to someone editing it in a shared document the day before. How should prompts that determine production behavior be managed?

options.A: Versioned, owned, reviewed, and evaluated on every change, as code is
options.B: Kept in a shared document with edit history, so every change is visible and reversible
options.C: Edited by whoever notices a problem, with a note posted in the team channel afterward
options.D: Frozen at launch and changed only through a formal annual revision process

architect-professional-mock3-13.rationale: Anything that determines production behavior needs the lifecycle of code: version control, ownership, review, and evaluation on change (A). A shared document (B) and ad hoc edits (C) allow unreviewed change, and freezing (D) blocks needed improvement.
architect-professional-mock3-13.evidence: Treat prompts as versioned artifacts and re-run evaluations whenever a prompt changes to catch regressions.

architect-professional-mock3-14.task: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
architect-professional-mock3-14.question: A CFO asks whether Claude Code is worth its license cost after six months. The usage dashboard shows thousands of sessions per week. What should be measured?

options.A: Weekly session and tool-invocation counts, trended per team against license spend
options.B: Change in the delivery outcomes the tool was adopted to improve, such as cycle time and escaped defects
options.C: The share of engineers onboarded and active each week against the rollout target
options.D: Hours spent in the tool per engineer, compared with time spent in the editor

architect-professional-mock3-14.rationale: Value is the outcome moved, not the activity generated: delivery outcomes the tool was adopted to improve (B). Session and invocation counts (A), adoption share (C), and hours in the tool (D) measure usage rather than benefit.
architect-professional-mock3-14.evidence: Usage telemetry shows adoption activity; business value must be judged against the outcomes the organization set out to improve.

architect-professional-mock3-15.task: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
architect-professional-mock3-15.question: A team working on a 600,000-line Java monolith finds that Claude Code produces changes that ignore their conventions and module boundaries. What most likely explains the poor results?

options.A: The repository is too large for Claude Code to work in at all, whatever context it is given
options.B: Java is less well supported than newer languages, which limits the quality of output on large codebases
options.C: The repository has no committed context, such as a CLAUDE.md, describing its conventions and module structure
options.D: Too many contributors commit to the repository, which makes its style inconsistent for the model

architect-professional-mock3-15.rationale: Missing project context is the usual cause, and the team can fix it by committing conventions and structure to project memory (C). Size (A), language (B), and contributor count (D) do not by themselves prevent good results.
architect-professional-mock3-15.evidence: Claude Code works best when CLAUDE.md documents project conventions, structure and commands so changes follow the codebase's norms.
